title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 18
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Passport Application Held Up
listeningScripts.text: Caller: I applied to renew my passport six weeks ago and the tracker still says in progress. Somebody told me I should ring. Officer: I can check that. Application reference? Caller: P-R-nine-nine-four-one-two-eight. Officer: Thank you. Right. It isn't in progress in the ordinary sense. It has been parked at the photograph check since the twelfth. Caller: Parked. Nobody has told me anything. Officer: They should have. A letter goes out when a photograph is rejected. But if a photograph is only queried, it sits in a queue for a second look, and no letter goes out for that. It's a gap we know about. Caller: What is wrong with the photograph? Officer: There is a shadow on the left of the face. Whether that fails depends on the assessor, which is why it has gone for a second pair of eyes rather than a straight rejection. Caller: How long does the second look take? Officer: It varies, and I won't pretend otherwise. The queue is running at about three weeks at the moment. Caller: Can I just send a new photograph? Officer: You can, and that is what I would do. Submitting a replacement pulls the application out of the query queue and puts it back into the main line, where the wait is currently eight working days. Caller: Doesn't it go to the back of the main line? Officer: It goes back to where it was by date. You don't lose the six weeks you have already waited. That's the part people assume wrongly and never ask about. Caller: How do I send it? Officer: Through the same online account, under add a document. Don't post it. A posted photograph goes to the scanning centre and takes eleven days to reach the file.

listeningScripts.title: Repair or Replace the Washing Machine
listeningScripts.text: A: The repair man has been. Ninety for the visit, and he says it's the drum bearings. B: Which costs what? A: Three hundred and twenty with the labour. And the machine is nine years old. B: A new one is what, five hundred? A: Five fifty for the same size. But the landlord replaced the last one, so I've emailed to ask. B: He won't. He didn't fix the extractor fan for four months. A: He might, if the alternative is a flooded kitchen. Anyway. If he says no, then three twenty on a nine-year-old machine is throwing money at it. B: Agreed. What about second-hand? There's a place on Beckett Street that reconditions them. Six-month warranty. A: How much? B: Two eighty, roughly, for something four or five years old. A: So two eighty for a machine with four years left in it, or five fifty for one with ten. That's the same money per year, and the new one doesn't need a van. B: Then new. We split it, and we take it with us when we go. A: We take it with us. Write that down somewhere, because in two years one of us will have forgotten.

listeningScripts.title: Volunteer Driver Programme Briefing
listeningScripts.text: Thank you all for coming. You will be driving neighbours to medical appointments, and there are six things you need to know before your first trip. Mileage. You claim it at the end of each month through the form, not by email, and the rate is fifty-eight cents a kilometre. It covers the whole journey, including getting to the client and getting yourself home again, which surprises people. A lot of volunteers have been claiming only the middle part. Insurance. Tell your insurer that you are doing volunteer driving. Almost every policy covers it at no extra cost, but almost every policy also requires you to have told them, and a policy you have not told is a policy that argues with you afterwards. You wait for the client. That is the part that catches people out. An appointment booked for forty minutes runs to ninety more often than not, and if you have gone, we have no way of getting that person home. If you genuinely cannot wait, say so when the trip is offered, not on the day. You do not go in. Not into the consulting room, not into the results conversation. If a client asks you to, and they will, the answer is that you will be right outside. That is not coldness. It is that you would be a witness to something you have no training to hear. No money changes hands. Not for petrol, not for a coffee, not a twenty pressed into your hand at the door. If somebody wants to give something, they give it to the office. And cancel through the office, never directly with the client. The client may forget to tell us, and then we send nobody.

listeningScripts.title: Rent Cap for Manufactured Home Parks
listeningScripts.text: British Columbia will cap annual rent increases for the pads beneath manufactured homes at the rate of inflation, removing an additional allowance that had let park owners add a further share of local government charges. About twelve thousand households rent a pad while owning the home standing on it, an arrangement the province describes as leaving residents unusually exposed. The home is theirs, but moving it is often impossible, because most homes built before the nineteen-nineties cannot survive being transported. Park owners' representatives said the additional allowance existed because utility and municipal costs rise faster than inflation, and that capping rents without addressing those costs will push some parks to close and redevelop. The province said park closures already require twelve months' notice and compensation, and that it will review the compensation formula this year — something residents' groups have been asking for since twenty-nineteen. The cap takes effect for increases issued after the first of July.

listeningScripts.title: Same-Day Appointment Slots
listeningScripts.text: Whitcombe: We hold twelve same-day slots a morning. On an average day four go unused, and meanwhile the routine list is four weeks out. Raman: They go unused because they are released at eight and they are gone by five past. The people who get them are the people who can ring at eight. Baptiste: Which is exactly who does not need them most. Anyone on a shift, anyone with a school run, anyone who cannot sit redialling for seven minutes. Whitcombe: If four are unused, then they are not all gone by five past. Raman: Both things are true. Eight are gone by five past, and four are never claimed at all, because by nine o'clock people have given up and stopped ringing. The slot exists and nobody can see it. Baptiste: Then show them. An online list that updates would let somebody at half past nine see that there is a slot at eleven. Whitcombe: We looked at that. The system can do it. What it cannot do is stop somebody booking a same-day slot for a thing that has already waited two months, and then the acutely unwell person has nowhere to go. Raman: That's a triage question, not a booking question. If a receptionist asks two questions before booking, it's solved. Whitcombe: It is solved, and it costs about forty seconds a call, which across a morning is another twenty minutes on the front desk. Baptiste: Then that is what the four wasted slots are worth. Twenty minutes of desk time against four appointments nobody used. Whitcombe: Put like that, I would take it. Let's trial it for six weeks and count both.

listeningScripts.title: Compulsory Cycle Helmets
listeningScripts.text: Whenever a city considers a cycling programme, somebody proposes a helmet law, and the argument that follows is one of the most confused in transport policy. Not because the evidence is thin, but because two different questions get answered as though they were one. The first question is whether a helmet protects the person wearing it in a crash. The answer is yes, clearly, for head injury, and anybody arguing otherwise is misreading the studies. If I come off my bike tomorrow, I would rather be wearing one. The second question is what a law requiring them does to a population, and that is a different thing entirely. In every jurisdiction that has made helmets compulsory for adults, cycling numbers fell — typically by a fifth to a third in the first years, and the fall was concentrated among occasional riders rather than committed ones. That matters because of a well-established relationship: the risk to each cyclist falls as the number of cyclists rises, because drivers adapt to expecting them. So a law that removes a third of the cyclists makes the road more dangerous for the ones who remain, which is the opposite of the intention. Then there is the health arithmetic, which is the part that decides it for me. The life-years lost to cycling head injuries are real, and they are small. The life-years lost to inactivity are enormous. A policy that trades a little head-injury risk for a measurable fall in cycling is losing that trade by a wide margin — even though the thing it prevents is far more visible than the thing it causes. So my position is this. Wear one, encourage them, provide them free to children, and do not make them compulsory for adults. The instinct behind the law is sound. It is the second question that the law answers badly.

questions.prompt: What is the true state of the application?
options: It was rejected and the file has been closed
It is in the main queue with eight days to run
It has been held at the photograph check since the twelfth
It was never received by the passport office
questions.correctAnswer: It has been held at the photograph check since the twelfth
questions.explanation: The tracker says in progress, but the officer explains it has been parked at the photograph check since the twelfth.

questions.prompt: Why was the caller not told?
options: Letters go out for a rejected photograph, not a queried one
The letter was sent to an old address
Letters are only sent after eight weeks
The tracker was meant to show it instead
questions.correctAnswer: Letters go out for a rejected photograph, not a queried one
questions.explanation: A rejection produces a letter; a query does not, and the officer calls that a gap the office knows about.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the photograph?
options: The face is too small in the frame
The background is the wrong colour
It was taken more than six months ago
There is a shadow on one side of the face
questions.correctAnswer: There is a shadow on one side of the face
questions.explanation: The officer describes a shadow on the left of the face, which may or may not fail depending on who assesses it.

questions.prompt: Why was it queried rather than rejected?
options: The applicant had already been written to once
Whether it fails depends on which assessor looks at it
Rejections are only issued after three weeks
A renewal cannot be rejected outright
questions.correctAnswer: Whether it fails depends on which assessor looks at it
questions.explanation: Because the shadow is a borderline case that depends on the assessor, the photograph went for a second pair of eyes instead of a straight rejection.

questions.prompt: How long is the queue for a second look?
options: Eight working days
Six weeks
About three weeks
Eleven days
questions.correctAnswer: About three weeks
questions.explanation: The officer gives about three weeks for the query queue, against eight working days for the main line.

questions.prompt: What does submitting a new photograph do?
options: It cancels the application and starts a new one
It shortens the query queue to eight days
It triggers the letter that was never sent
It moves the application back into the main queue
questions.correctAnswer: It moves the application back into the main queue
questions.explanation: A replacement photograph pulls the application out of the query queue and returns it to the main line, where the wait is eight working days.

questions.prompt: What happens to the six weeks already waited?
options: They are kept, because the application returns to its place by date
They are lost, and the wait restarts
They count only if the photograph is accepted
They are added to the eight working days
questions.correctAnswer: They are kept, because the application returns to its place by date
questions.explanation: The officer says the application goes back to where it was by date, so the six weeks are not lost — the assumption people make and never check.

questions.prompt: Why should the photograph not be posted?
options: Posted photographs are not accepted at all
A posted photograph takes eleven days to reach the file
The scanning centre returns them to the sender
Only the online account records the date
questions.correctAnswer: A posted photograph takes eleven days to reach the file
questions.explanation: Posting sends the photograph via the scanning centre, adding eleven days before it reaches the file, so the online account is the route to use.

questions.prompt: What has the repair man diagnosed?
options: The drum bearings
A blocked pump
A leaking door seal
A failed motor
questions.correctAnswer: The drum bearings
questions.explanation: The visit cost ninety dollars and the fault is the drum bearings, at three hundred and twenty with labour.

questions.prompt: What has A already done?
options: Ordered a new machine online
Booked a second repair visit
Emailed the landlord to ask about a replacement
Arranged to borrow a neighbour's machine
questions.correctAnswer: Emailed the landlord to ask about a replacement
questions.explanation: A has emailed the landlord, on the grounds that the landlord replaced the last machine.

questions.prompt: Why does B doubt the landlord will help?
options: He has already refused once this year
He left the extractor fan unrepaired for four months
The machine is not his responsibility
He is selling the property
questions.correctAnswer: He left the extractor fan unrepaired for four months
questions.explanation: B's evidence is the extractor fan, which went unfixed for four months.

questions.prompt: What does A conclude about the reconditioned machine?
options: The warranty is too short to be useful
It is cheaper than any other option
It would not fit the space
It works out at the same cost per year as a new one
questions.correctAnswer: It works out at the same cost per year as a new one
questions.explanation: Two eighty for four years against five fifty for ten comes to the same money per year — and the new one does not need a van.

questions.prompt: What do they agree to do?
options: Wait for the landlord's reply before deciding
Buy a new machine, split the cost, and take it when they move
Have the bearings replaced after all
Buy the reconditioned machine from Beckett Street
questions.correctAnswer: Buy a new machine, split the cost, and take it when they move
questions.explanation: They settle on a new machine, split between them and taken with them when they leave — which A wants written down.

questions.prompt: How is mileage claimed?
options: By email after each trip
In cash from the office
It is paid automatically
On a form at the end of each month
questions.correctAnswer: On a form at the end of each month
questions.explanation: Mileage is claimed monthly through the form rather than by email, at fifty-eight cents a kilometre.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say surprises volunteers about mileage?
options: It is paid at a higher rate in winter
It covers getting to the client and getting home again
It is capped at a set number of kilometres
It has to be claimed within a week
questions.correctAnswer: It covers getting to the client and getting home again
questions.explanation: The rate covers the whole journey, including reaching the client and returning home, though many volunteers have been claiming only the middle part.

questions.prompt: What does the insurance point come down to?
options: The insurer has to have been told
Volunteer driving costs extra on most policies
The programme insures drivers itself
Only fully comprehensive policies are accepted
questions.correctAnswer: The insurer has to have been told
questions.explanation: Almost every policy covers volunteer driving at no extra cost, but almost every policy requires having been told — and an untold policy argues with you afterwards.

questions.prompt: When should a driver say they cannot wait?
options: As soon as the appointment overruns
Only if the appointment exceeds ninety minutes
When the trip is offered, rather than on the day
By telling the client directly
questions.correctAnswer: When the trip is offered, rather than on the day
questions.explanation: Drivers are expected to wait, since a forty-minute appointment often runs to ninety; anyone who genuinely cannot must say so when the trip is offered.

questions.prompt: Why must a driver not go into the appointment?
options: The clinic does not allow visitors
It would extend the appointment
The programme's insurance does not cover it
They would hear something they have no training to hear
questions.correctAnswer: They would hear something they have no training to hear
questions.explanation: The rule is not coldness: a driver in the room becomes a witness to something they have no training to hear, so the answer to a client who asks is that you will be right outside.

questions.prompt: Why must cancellations go through the office?
options: The office keeps a record for insurance
Clients cannot cancel at short notice
The client may not pass the message on
The driver would not be paid otherwise
questions.correctAnswer: The client may not pass the message on
questions.explanation: Cancelling directly with the client risks the client forgetting to tell the office, and then nobody is sent.

questions.prompt: What is being capped?
options: The price at which a manufactured home can be sold
The charges levied by local government
The rent charged for the pad beneath a home
The cost of moving a manufactured home
questions.correctAnswer: The rent charged for the pad beneath a home
questions.explanation: The cap applies to annual rent increases for the pads beneath manufactured homes, holding them to the rate of inflation.

questions.prompt: What is being removed?
options: An allowance for passing on local government charges
The requirement to give notice of closure
The compensation paid when a park closes
The right to raise rents at all
questions.correctAnswer: An allowance for passing on local government charges
questions.explanation: The additional allowance had let park owners add a further share of local government charges on top of inflation, and it goes.

questions.prompt: Why does the province call residents unusually exposed?
options: They have no written tenancy agreements
They own homes that usually cannot be moved
They pay rent on both the home and the pad
They cannot sell without the owner's consent
questions.correctAnswer: They own homes that usually cannot be moved
questions.explanation: Residents own the home but rent the ground, and most homes built before the nineteen-nineties cannot survive being transported, so leaving is not a real option.

questions.prompt: What did park owners' representatives argue?
options: Twelve thousand is an overestimate of the households affected
Residents would be better served by buying their pads
The cap should start later than the first of July
Their utility and municipal costs rise faster than inflation
questions.correctAnswer: Their utility and municipal costs rise faster than inflation
questions.explanation: The owners' case is that the allowance existed because utility and municipal costs outpace inflation, and that a cap without addressing those costs will push parks to close and redevelop.

questions.prompt: What did the province offer in response?
options: A review of the compensation formula this year
A delay to the start of the cap
A subsidy for park owners' utility costs
An exemption for smaller parks
questions.correctAnswer: A review of the compensation formula this year
questions.explanation: The province pointed to the existing twelve months' notice and compensation on closure, and undertook to review the compensation formula this year — a review residents' groups have sought since twenty-nineteen.

questions.prompt: What problem does Whitcombe describe?
options: Twelve slots a morning is too few for demand
Four same-day slots go unused while routine patients wait four weeks
The routine list has grown to four weeks because of the same-day slots
Patients book same-day slots and do not attend
questions.correctAnswer: Four same-day slots go unused while routine patients wait four weeks
questions.explanation: Whitcombe opens with twelve same-day slots a morning, four of them unused on an average day, against a routine list running four weeks out.

questions.prompt: What is Raman's explanation?
options: Patients do not know the slots exist at all
The slots are held back for regular patients
Receptionists give them out inconsistently
They are released at eight and taken within minutes
questions.correctAnswer: They are released at eight and taken within minutes
questions.explanation: Raman says the slots are released at eight and gone by five past, so they go to whoever is able to ring at eight.

questions.prompt: What is Baptiste's objection?
options: Eight in the morning is too early for a surgery to open
Same-day slots should be booked online only
The people able to ring at eight are not those in most need
The routine list should be cleared first
questions.correctAnswer: The people able to ring at eight are not those in most need
questions.explanation: Baptiste's point is who is excluded by a phone queue at eight: anyone on a shift, with a school run, or unable to sit redialling for seven minutes.

questions.prompt: How can both of the first two statements be true?
options: Eight go immediately and four are never claimed because people give up
The four unused slots are on different days
Some patients book and then cancel
The twelve slots are counted across two mornings
questions.correctAnswer: Eight go immediately and four are never claimed because people give up
questions.explanation: Raman reconciles them: eight go by five past, and the remaining four are never claimed because by nine o'clock people have stopped ringing — the slot exists but nobody can see it.

questions.prompt: What does Baptiste propose?
options: Releasing the slots later in the day
An online list that updates through the morning
Holding slots back for shift workers
Adding more staff to answer the phones at eight
questions.correctAnswer: An online list that updates through the morning
questions.explanation: Baptiste suggests showing the unclaimed slots, so somebody at half past nine can see there is one at eleven.

questions.prompt: What is Whitcombe's concern about that?
options: Non-urgent problems would take the slots
The practice's system cannot display live availability
Older patients would be unable to use it
It would need approval from the health authority
questions.correctAnswer: Non-urgent problems would take the slots
questions.explanation: Whitcombe accepts the system can do it, but says it cannot stop somebody booking a same-day slot for something that has already waited two months, leaving the acutely unwell with nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: What is Raman's answer to that concern?
options: Restricting the online list to certain patients
Keeping four slots off the online list
Reviewing bookings at the end of each morning
Two questions asked at the desk before booking
questions.correctAnswer: Two questions asked at the desk before booking
questions.explanation: Raman calls it a triage question rather than a booking one: a receptionist asking two questions before booking solves it.

questions.prompt: What settles the argument?
options: The health authority's guidance on triage
A vote among the practice's partners
Twenty minutes of desk time weighed against four unused appointments
The cost of changing the booking system
questions.correctAnswer: Twenty minutes of desk time weighed against four unused appointments
questions.explanation: Baptiste puts the trade plainly — twenty minutes of front-desk time against four appointments nobody used — and Whitcombe accepts it on those terms, with a six-week trial counting both.

questions.prompt: Which two questions does the speaker say get confused?
options: Whether a helmet protects a rider, and what a law does to a population
Whether helmets work, and whether they are affordable
Whether cycling is safe, and whether drivers are at fault
Whether children and adults should be treated alike
questions.correctAnswer: Whether a helmet protects a rider, and what a law does to a population
questions.explanation: The speaker's framing is that the debate answers two different questions as though they were one: the protective effect on an individual, and the population effect of a law.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about the first question?
options: The studies on it contradict one another
The protection is smaller than campaigners claim
A helmet clearly protects against head injury
It matters only at higher speeds
questions.correctAnswer: A helmet clearly protects against head injury
questions.explanation: On the first question the speaker is unequivocal: helmets protect against head injury, and anyone arguing otherwise is misreading the studies.

questions.prompt: What has happened where adult helmet laws have been introduced?
options: Head injuries fell by a fifth to a third
Cycling numbers recovered within a year
The fall was largest among people who already wore helmets
Cycling numbers fell by a fifth to a third
questions.correctAnswer: Cycling numbers fell by a fifth to a third
questions.explanation: In every jurisdiction with a compulsory adult law, cycling fell — typically a fifth to a third in the first years — with the fall concentrated among occasional rather than committed riders.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say that makes cycling more dangerous?
options: The remaining cyclists ride faster
Roads get safer for each cyclist as more people ride
Helmets encourage drivers to pass more closely
Fewer cyclists means less spending on cycle lanes
questions.correctAnswer: Roads get safer for each cyclist as more people ride
questions.explanation: The established relationship is that risk per cyclist falls as numbers rise, because drivers adapt to expecting them — so removing a third of cyclists makes the road worse for those who remain.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say decides the question?
options: The life-years lost to inactivity outweigh those lost to head injuries
The cost of enforcing a helmet law
The difficulty of proving that helmets work
The number of cyclists who already wear one
questions.correctAnswer: The life-years lost to inactivity outweigh those lost to head injuries
questions.explanation: The health arithmetic decides it: head-injury life-years are real but small, inactivity life-years are enormous, and the trade is lost by a wide margin even though the harm prevented is more visible than the harm caused.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's position?
options: Make helmets compulsory only for occasional riders
Delay any law until better evidence exists
Compel adults but not children
Encourage helmets and give them to children, but do not compel adults
questions.correctAnswer: Encourage helmets and give them to children, but do not compel adults
questions.explanation: The speaker would wear one, encourage them and provide them free to children, while opposing a compulsory adult law — the instinct is sound, but the law answers the second question badly.
